{{Short description|1979 single by Robert John}} {{Infobox song | name = Sad Eyes | image = Sad eyes by robert john US vinyl.png | alt = | caption = Side A of US single | type = single | artist = [[Robert John]] | album = [[Robert John (album)|Robert John]] | B-side = Am I Ever Gonna Hold You Again | released = April 1979 | recorded = 1979 | studio = | venue = | genre = * [[Soft rock]]{{cite book|title= Night Moves - Pop Music in the Late 70s|first1=Don|last1=Breithaupt|first2= Jeff|last2= Breithaupt|date= July 17, 2000|chapter= The Linen: Soft Rock|page= 112|publisher=[[St. Martin's Press|St. Martin's Griffin]]|isbn=978-0-312-19821-3|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kh04AwAAQBAJ&pg=PT95}}{{cite web|first= Tom |last= Breihan |title= The Number Ones: Robert John's "Sad Eyes"|website= [[Stereogum]] |date= February 19, 2020 |url= https://www.stereogum.com/2073765/the-number-ones-robert-johns-sad-eyes/columns/the-number-ones/|quote= The song essentially sounds like a doo-wop ballad, filtered through early-’70s soft-rock...|accessdate= July 12, 2023}} * [[doo-wop]]{{cite web|first= Tom |last= Breihan |title= The Number Ones: Robert John's "Sad Eyes"|website= [[Stereogum]] |date= February 19, 2020 |url= https://www.stereogum.com/2073765/the-number-ones-robert-johns-sad-eyes/columns/the-number-ones/|quote= The song essentially sounds like a doo-wop ballad, filtered through early-’70s soft-rock...|accessdate= July 12, 2023}} | length = 4:12 (Album Version)
3:30 (Single Edit) | label = [[EMI America Records|EMI America]] | writer = Robert John | producer = [[George Tobin]] in association with [[Mike Piccirillo]] | prev_title = [[Hushabye]] | prev_year = 1972 | next_title = Only Time | next_year = 1979 }} "'''Sad Eyes'''" is a song written and recorded by [[Robert John]], and released in April 1979. It debuted May 19 on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], reaching the top of the chart the week of October 6.[https://www.billboard.com/charts/hot-100/1979-10-06/?rank=1 ''Billboard'' Hot 100, week of October 6, 1979 – Billboard.com.] Retrieved January 28, 2023. It was produced by George Tobin in association with Mike Piccirillo. Reminiscent of the doo-wop ballads of the 1950s, "Sad Eyes" was released in April 1979. "Sad Eyes" is notable as the song that ended the six-week reign of the biggest smash hit of the year, [[The Knack]]'s "[[My Sharona]]". This song explores the sadness experienced by a woman because her lover is leaving to return to his girlfriend/wife. The lyrics indicate that the relationship was intended from the start to be a temporary one that would end upon the girlfriend’s return. The song is told from the man’s point of view and expresses his efforts to console her.

sections.heading: Cover versions
sections.wikitext: A cover by American [[country music]] group [[Trader-Price]] peaked at number 55 on the ''Billboard'' [[Hot Country Songs|Hot Country Singles]] chart in 1989.<ref name="whitburn2013">{{cite book|last=Whitburn|first=Joel|title=Hot Country Songs 1944–2012|publisher=Record Research, Inc|page=339|year=2013|isbn=978-0-89820-203-8}}</ref> [[Kyle Vincent]] also recorded the song, released on ''Absolutely The Best of the 70s'', credited to [[Bo Donaldson and The Heywoods]], and produced by [[Ron Dante]].  Another rendition appeared on [[Robin Lee (singer)|Robin Lee]]'s album, ''[[Black Velvet (Robin Lee album)|Black Velvet]]'', released in 1990.
sections.text: A cover by American country music group Trader-Price peaked at number 55 on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart in 1989. Kyle Vincent also recorded the song, released on Absolutely The Best of the 70s, credited to Bo Donaldson and The Heywoods, and produced by Ron Dante.  Another rendition appeared on Robin Lee's album, Black Velvet, released in 1990.
